tooltip.title: Classification of Chronic Pruritus
tooltip.markdown: Chronic itch is broadly categorized based on its underlying origin, following the classification system proposed by the International Forum for the Study of Itch (IFSI).

tooltip.title: Dermatologic Pruritus
tooltip.markdown: Itch arising from a primary inflammatory or infectious skin disease. This is the most common cause of chronic pruritus.

tooltip.title: Eczematous Dermatitis
tooltip.markdown: Includes Atopic Dermatitis ("the itch that rashes"), Contact Dermatitis, and Xerotic Eczema (dry skin).

tooltip.title: Infections and Infestations
tooltip.markdown: Scabies is a key diagnosis to consider in any patient with severe, nocturnal itch.

tooltip.title: Autoimmune Blistering Diseases
tooltip.markdown: Bullous Pemphigoid can present with intense pruritus and urticarial plaques for months before blisters appear, especially in the elderly.

tooltip.title: Systemic Pruritus
tooltip.markdown: Itch as a manifestation of an internal disease. It typically presents as generalized pruritus without a primary rash.

tooltip.title: Chronic Kidney Disease-Associated Pruritus (CKD-aP)
tooltip.markdown: Common in patients on dialysis. Often severe, generalized, and worse at night.

tooltip.title: Cholestatic Pruritus
tooltip.markdown: Caused by impaired bile flow (e.g., primary biliary cholangitis). Often starts on palms and soles.

tooltip.title: Hematologic and Malignant Causes
tooltip.markdown: **Polycythemia Vera:** presents with aquagenic pruritus (itching after contact with water). **Lymphoma (esp. Hodgkin):** can present with severe, nocturnal pruritus and B-symptoms.

tooltip.title: Endocrine Causes
tooltip.markdown: Hyperthyroidism, and less commonly, diabetes mellitus and hypothyroidism can be associated with generalized pruritus.

tooltip.title: Neuropathic Pruritus
tooltip.markdown: Itch caused by injury or dysfunction of the afferent nervous system. Often localized to a specific dermatome and accompanied by other sensations like burning or stinging.

tooltip.title: Brachioradial Pruritus
tooltip.markdown: Itch on the dorsolateral forearms, thought to be from cervical spine disease (C5-C7). Classically improves with application of ice (the "ice-pack sign").

tooltip.title: Notalgia Paresthetica
tooltip.markdown: Unilateral itch on the mid-upper back (medial to the scapula), from nerve entrapment of T2-T6 spinal nerves.

tooltip.title: Post-herpetic Pruritus
tooltip.markdown: Chronic itch that persists in a dermatome after an episode of herpes zoster (shingles).

tooltip.title: Psychogenic Pruritus
tooltip.markdown: Itch related to a primary psychiatric disorder. This is a diagnosis of exclusion. Includes conditions like delusional infestation.

tooltip.title: Chronic Pruritus of Unknown Origin (CPUO)
tooltip.markdown: A diagnosis of exclusion for patients with chronic itch lasting >6 weeks where a thorough workup reveals no dermatologic, systemic, neuropathic, or psychogenic cause.
